new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states where word stress falls. The only accessible phonological description (Lander-Portnoy 2013) explicitly leaves stress unstudied and says its role is unknown. The primary sketch (Dondrup 1990, quoted second-hand) claims Bugun has two contrastive tones, rising vs falling, with four minimal pairs; Lander-Portnoy's pitch measurements on three tokens contradict Dondrup in two of three and he calls the tone system erroneous or unproven. Barbora 2025 (paywalled) says its sketch covers 'tone'.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the tone claim itself is disputed (Lander-Portnoy 2013 pp. 28-29: 'Dondrup's system is erroneous either in its description of the tonal system in Bugun or fundamentally in its prediction of phonemic tones or pitches').
new_statements.domain_note: Monosyllabic citation forms (Dondrup's minimal pairs kho, chau, kua, chai); Lander-Portnoy's data are isolated words from the 2011 Enduring Voices recordings (Bugun Talking Dictionary). Nothing on phrase-level prosody.
new_statements.identity_note: Lander-Portnoy 2013 describes Bugun as recorded by the 2011 Enduring Voices expedition (village given as 'Rama Bao', possibly Ramu, Singchung circle); Lieberherr & Bodt 2017 distinguish Singchung and Bichom varieties; Barbora 2025 draws on three villages. All fall under bugu1246; no dialect-level glottocodes exist. Dondrup 1990 is the 'Handbook on Bugun Language Guide' named by the earlier scan.

sources.note: Sec. 5 Suprasegmentals, 5.2 Stress (p. 28): stress is explicitly 'beyond the scope of this paper'; 5.3 (pp. 28-29) reports Dondrup 1990's claim of two contrastive tones (rising vs falling, four minimal pairs) and finds pitch tracks of three tokens match Dondrup in only one case, calling his tone system erroneous; conclusion p. 30: 'The role of tone and stress in the language is yet unknown'. No statement of where stress falls.
